IM10-01.note: 180 = 2^2*3^2*5; distinct primes 2+3+5=10. 'Distinct' is stated, so the 15 (with repetition) trap is fair rather than ambiguous. Every distractor is a named path: repetition, counting 1 as prime, multiplying instead of adding.

IM10-02.note: 12*9/2 = 54. Genuinely hard for ISEE Upper: the student must either know n(n-3)/2 or derive it and remember to halve. 108 (unhalved) and 66 (all segments, sides included) are the two errors this item actually produces.

IM10-03.note: 10 x 10^5 renormalised to 1 x 10^6. The renormalisation carry is the whole item, and 100000/10000 are exactly the two ways to botch it. Options are given as plain integers while the stem is in scientific notation - not ambiguous, but it removes the 'match the exponent' shortcut, which is good.

IM10-04.note: Mode = value with highest frequency = 3. The '5' (reporting the frequency 5 rather than the value) is the strong distractor and is doing real work because 5 is also a legal value in the table. '2' (value with lowest frequency) is the weak one - no student computes a minimum here.

IM10-05.note: 0.35 x 360 = 126. '35' (percent read as degrees) and '63' (half-circle) are real; '105' requires the student to invent 3 degrees per percent, which is a rounding of 3.6 nobody performs deliberately - it is the weak leg.

IM10-06.note: The linear factor applies twice: 108 sq ft / 9 = 12 sq yd. '36' (divided by 3 once) is THE error this topic exists to catch, and '108' catches the student who never converts. Textbook construction.

IM10-07.note: 2000 x 1.1^2. '2400' is simple interest, '2200' is one year, '2662' is three years - the three canonical compound-interest slips, and the 10% rate keeps the arithmetic clean enough that the concept is what is tested.

IM10-08.note: 2(3.14)(25) + 2(3.14)(5)(10) = 157 + 314 = 471. Commissioned hard, grades medium: 'closed can' and 'total surface area' both spell out that the ends count, and pi is supplied, so this is formula recall plus two multiplications. '392.5' (one end only) is the sharpest distractor; '785' is the volume, which is the error students actually make.

IM10-09.note: (-3,5) -> (-3,-5) -> (1,-5), sum -4. Asking for the coordinate SUM rather than the point is what makes the distractors work: '12' is the y-axis reflection, '2' is the origin, '-12' is the wrong translation direction. Each is a distinct named transformation error.

IM10-10.note: -12/6 = -2. The four options are exactly {slope, negated slope, reciprocal, negated reciprocal}, which is the complete error lattice for this skill. Two negative coordinates keep it above easy.

IM10-11.note: B = (2*2-(-4), 2*(-1)-3) = (8,-5), sum 3. Commissioned hard, grades medium - reversing the midpoint formula is a standard ISEE Upper item, and the negative coordinates are the only real friction. The '2' distractor (M - A, the displacement, stopping one step short) is the one most students will land on.

IM10-12.note: (1/3)(3.14)(36)(10) = 376.8. Commissioned hard but the stem supplies both the formula and pi, which drops it to arithmetic - medium. '1130.4' (no one-third) and '1507.2' (diameter for radius) are strong; '904.32' is the sphere volume, which almost no student reaches when the cone formula is printed in the stem - the weak leg.

IM10-13.note: x = 8 and x = -3, sum 5. '8' (positive branch only) is the dominant real error, '16' forgets to divide by 2, '2.5' averages. Asking for the sum rather than the solution set is what lets the single-branch error be scored.

IM10-14.note: 4n > 56 so n > 14, least integer 15. '14' (strict vs non-strict) is the point of the item and is strong. '11' (dropping the -15) is real. '28' requires dividing 56 by 2 rather than 4, which is not an error this stem invites - the weak leg.

IM10-15.note: 1200 x 3/8 = 450. '150' (one eighth, stopping early) and '400' (dividing by 3, using the wrong half of the ratio) are both errors seen constantly at this level; '360' is a tenths-vs-eighths slip. Clean easy item.

IM10-16.note: 45 mod 7 = 3, three days past Tuesday. Every distractor is a named modular error: quotient-for-remainder (Monday), counting backward (Saturday), inclusive counting (Thursday). The word-valued options also mean the numeric cross-item patterns cannot touch this one.

IM10-17.note: 24 - 15 = 9. '15' (old range) and '24' (new range) are the two errors of reading 'increase' as 'value', and they carry the item. '21' is justified as taking 9 for the minimum when 6 is plainly in the set; it is also, awkwardly, the value that was replaced, so a student may select it by recognition rather than by any error - the weak leg.

IM10-18.note: 53 - 32 = 21. Once the plot is read the arithmetic is one subtraction, so this is easy against the real exam despite the unfamiliar display. '2' (stems only) is the genuine plot-misreading distractor; '9' (the count) and '15' (53 - 38) are thinner.

IM10-19.note: 12 parts over 180 gives 15 per part, largest = 105. '126' (summing the parts as 10) and '75' (the other two angles combined) are real. '84' = 7 x 12 asks the student to multiply by the part COUNT instead of the part SIZE, which is a stated but not a natural error - the weak leg.

IM10-20.note: 1/8 + 1/3 = 11/24. '1/11' (reciprocal of the sum of the bases) is the classic negative-exponent error and is worth the item on its own; '5/6' reads 2^(-3) as 1/2. Note the key is the only two-digit numerator among the options, but that is arithmetic necessity, not a tell - it is the only one of the four that could be a sum of eighths and thirds.

IM10-21.note: |8 - (-13)| = 21. '22' (counting integers inclusive rather than measuring the gap) is the error this item is built for and is excellent; the two mirror-image distractors cover students who fold one point about zero.

IM10-22.note: 126/360 = 7/20; the three angles sum to exactly 360, so the stem is self-consistent and the fairness assumption is the standard one. '1/3' (equal sectors) is the strong distractor, '2/5' answers for the wrong sector, '7/40' doubles the circle. Reduction to lowest terms is required, which is where the real difficulty sits.

IM10-23.note: Sorted: 3,5,8,12,20,30; median (8+12)/2 = 10. Adding a sixth value forces the even-count average, which is the skill. '14' (averaging positions 3 and 4 of the UNSORTED list) is the sharpest distractor in the batch - it punishes exactly the student who does not re-sort.

IM10-24.note: side 11, perimeter 44. '11' (stopping at the side) is the real error and is strong; '22' and '121' are thinner - restating the area is a slip of attention rather than a method error.

IM10-25.note: Same-side interior angles are supplementary: 5x + 10 = 180, x = 34. '36' (dropping the constant) and '38' (sign on the constant) are the two algebra slips; '16' is the supplementary/complementary confusion. Note it asks for x, not the angle, which blocks answering by eyeballing a figure - and no figure is supplied, so nothing can be read off a drawing.

IM10-26.note: 6^2 = 36 through 17^2 = 289, so 17 - 6 + 1 = 12. Hardest item in the batch alongside IM10-02: the student must bracket both ends by trial and then count inclusively. '11' (forgetting the +1) is the dominant error and '17' (reporting the root) the second. 'Between' is unambiguous here since neither 30 nor 300 is a square.

IM10-27.note: Increases are 450, 730, 530, 290; the greatest is 730. '450' (first pair only) and '530' (a different pair) are attention errors rather than method errors; '820' (a two-year span) is the one real trap, since 'from one year to the next' is the constraint being tested. Four subtractions with no shortcut is what keeps it out of easy.

IM10-28.note: LCM(4,6) = 12, first three-digit multiple 108. The distractor set is ideal: 100 satisfies only the 4, 102 satisfies only the 6, and 120 uses the product 24 instead of the LCM. A student who checks only one divisor is caught either way.

IM10-29.note: 6 degrees per minute x 25 = 150. '90' (calling 25 minutes a quarter of the dial) is the strong distractor because 25 is deliberately close to 15, and '12.5' is the hour-hand rate. The rate 6 deg/min is not stated, which is what lifts this above easy.

IM10-30.note: sqrt(625 - 49) = sqrt(576) = 24. Commissioned hard but 7-24-25 is one of the memorised triples and the stem names the hypotenuse explicitly, so it grades medium. '18' (subtracting sides instead of squares) is the strong distractor; '12.5' (half the hypotenuse) corresponds to no error at this level and is the weak leg.

_batch_note: Cross-item check, since a tell across items is invisible from inside one: key letter spread is 7/8/8/7 over slots A-D, the key's value rank among its four options is 6/7/9/7 from smallest to largest, and the key is uniquely the longest option in only 2 of 30 - so none of letter position, magnitude rank, or option length identifies the answer. Reading the option sets with the stems covered, the numbers alone do not decide any item: every set is four bare quantities in the same frame, which is the clean pattern for maths (an option set only leaks when the options differ along the axis the stem names, and these do not). The one recurring authoring shape is asking for a derived aggregate rather than the object found ('sum of the coordinates' in IM10-09 and IM10-11, 'sum of the two values' in IM10-13, 'by how much does the range increase' in IM10-17); this is good practice, not a tell, because it does not make the answer predictable - but it does mean a student who learns partway through that the batch never wants the intermediate object gains a small hint to re-read the question, so do not push this device further in the next set. Difficulty: 0 items graded false on exclusivity, and my difficulty grades come out 7 easy / 21 medium / 2 hard against the batch's 6 / 17 / 7. Five of the seven commissioned hard (IM10-08, 11, 12, 19, 30) grade medium, mostly because the stem supplies the formula and the constant (12), names the configuration explicitly (08), or rests on a memorised triple (30). Only IM10-02 and IM10-26 are hard against the real ISEE. That is a batch-level finding, not a defect in any single item.
